description:

The colouring is built one vertex at a time. At each step the policy picks which uncoloured vertex to colour next; that vertex then automatically gets the smallest colour (colours are numbered 0, 1, 2, ...) not already used by one of its coloured neighbours. A new colour is opened only when every existing colour is taken by some neighbour. So the policy decides only the **order**, and the order decides how many colours are needed.

One **decision** = choosing the next vertex. The **candidates** are all uncoloured vertices, in index order. Vertices are numbered at random, so the index carries no information. When one vertex is left it is taken automatically.

Four training families: `sparse` (random graphs, 120 vertices, each pair joined with probability 0.08), `dense` (random, 70 vertices, probability 0.5), `geometric` (120 random points in the unit square, joined when closer than 0.25) and `planted` (100 vertices secretly split into 6 groups; pairs in different groups are joined with probability 0.35, pairs in the same group never, so 6 colours suffice). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is colours used / the fewest colours known for that graph - 1, in % (for `planted`, the known 6 or fewer). Colour counts are small integers, so one colour more or less moves an instance's gap by roughly 10-25%.

metric_notes.largest_class_pct: % of vertices in the largest colour class
metric_notes.smallest_class: size of the smallest colour class
metric_notes.singleton_classes: colour classes with a single vertex
metric_notes.last_color_at_pct: how far into the order (%) the highest colour was first opened
metric_notes.colors_at_half: colours in use when half of the vertices are coloured
metric_notes.deg_rank_corr: correlation between a vertex's degree and how early it was coloured (+1 = high degree first)

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Graph colouring: choose the order to colour vertices

Colour every vertex of a graph so that no two adjacent vertices share a colour, using as few colours as possible.

The colouring is built one vertex at a time. At each step the policy picks which uncoloured vertex to colour next; that vertex then automatically gets the smallest colour (colours are numbered 0, 1, 2, ...) not already used by one of its coloured neighbours. A new colour is opened only when every existing colour is taken by some neighbour. So the policy decides only the **order**, and the order decides how many colours are needed.

One **decision** = choosing the next vertex. The **candidates** are all uncoloured vertices, in index order. Vertices are numbered at random, so the index carries no information. When one vertex is left it is taken automatically.

Four training families: `sparse` (random graphs, 120 vertices, each pair joined with probability 0.08), `dense` (random, 70 vertices, probability 0.5), `geometric` (120 random points in the unit square, joined when closer than 0.25) and `planted` (100 vertices secretly split into 6 groups; pairs in different groups are joined with probability 0.35, pairs in the same group never, so 6 colours suffice). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is colours used / the fewest colours known for that graph - 1, in % (for `planted`, the known 6 or fewer). Colour counts are small integers, so one colour more or less moves an instance's gap by roughly 10-25%.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `neighbor_colors`: shape (k, c), int: for each candidate (uncoloured vertex, index order) and each colour used so far, how many of its neighbours already have that colour. c = number of colours used so far (c = 0 at the first decision: the array has shape (k, 0)). The colour a candidate would get is the first column that is 0 in its row, or c (a new colour) if none is.
- `adjacency`: shape (k, k), bool: which candidates are adjacent to each other (the graph restricted to the uncoloured vertices; symmetric, False on the diagonal).
- `degree`: shape (k,), int: each candidate's degree in the whole graph (coloured + uncoloured neighbours).
- `color_sizes`: shape (c,), int: how many vertices have each colour so far.
- The whole graph has n = k + color_sizes.sum() vertices.
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c')). The highest-scoring candidate is coloured next.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

import numpy as np
import math

def priority(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):

    total = None
    for f, w in _TERMS:
        v = np.asarray(f(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes), dtype=float)

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Fraction of each candidate's uncoloured neighbours that are adjacent to each other (local density among the still-uncoloured)."""
    k = adjacency.shape[0]
    if k == 0:
        return np.zeros(0)
    uncolored_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    # number of edges among neighbours of v, via adjacency^2 restricted appropriately
    a = adjacency.astype(float)
    tri = np.einsum('ij,ij->i', a @ a, a)  # twice the number of triangles through v
    triangles = 0.5 * tri
    denom = uncolored_deg * (uncolored_deg - 1.0)
    density = np.where(denom > 0, 2.0 * triangles / np.maximum(denom, 1.0), 0.0)
    return np.nan_to_num(density, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0)
```

import numpy as np
import math

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Saturation scaled by the fraction of uncoloured neighbours already coloured, reward for candidates that sit in a small closed neighbourhood."""
    k = neighbor_colors.shape[0]
    if neighbor_colors.shape[1] == 0:
        # no colours yet: use degree-based signal
        d = degree.astype(float)
        return (d - d.mean()) / (d.std() + 1e-9)
    sat = (neighbor_colors > 0).sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    colored_neigh = neighbor_colors.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    uncolored_neigh = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    total_neigh = colored_neigh + uncolored_neigh
    frac_colored = colored_neigh / (total_neigh + 1e-9)
    # reward high saturation concentrated in a small neighbourhood
    closed = total_neigh + 1.0
    val = sat * frac_colored / np.sqrt(closed)
    m = val.mean()
    s = val.std()
    return (val - m) / (s + 1e-9)
```

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Fraction of a candidate's colour-closed neighbourhood already saturated by each forbidden colour, weighted by how tight the fit is (DSATUR-like pressure blended with saturation density)."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape

    sat = (neighbor_colors > 0).sum(axis=1).astype(float)

    uncol_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    # total neighbours = coloured (sum of row) + uncoloured
    coloured_deg = neighbor_colors.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    total_deg = coloured_deg + uncol_deg
    # saturation ratio: how close to being fully blocked across used colours
    sat_ratio = sat / np.maximum(c, 1.0)
    # tightness: fraction of neighbour mass concentrated on already-used colours
    used_mass = np.where(neighbor_colors > 0, neighbor_colors, 0).sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    tight = used_mass / np.maximum(coloured_deg, 1.0)
    # conflict density: coloured neighbours per total neighbour
    density = coloured_deg / np.maximum(total_deg, 1.0)
    # combine: high saturation, high tightness, low remaining uncoloured degree pressure
    val = sat_ratio * tight + 0.5 * density
    return np.clip(val, 0.0, 1.0)

    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape

    """Negative (normalised) size of the smallest existing colour class the candidate can legally join; forced-new-colour candidates get -1."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape

# The problem: Graph colouring: choose the order to colour vertices

Colour every vertex of a graph so that no two adjacent vertices share a colour, using as few colours as possible.

The colouring is built one vertex at a time. At each step the policy picks which uncoloured vertex to colour next; that vertex then automatically gets the smallest colour (colours are numbered 0, 1, 2, ...) not already used by one of its coloured neighbours. A new colour is opened only when every existing colour is taken by some neighbour. So the policy decides only the **order**, and the order decides how many colours are needed.

One **decision** = choosing the next vertex. The **candidates** are all uncoloured vertices, in index order. Vertices are numbered at random, so the index carries no information. When one vertex is left it is taken automatically.

Four training families: `sparse` (random graphs, 120 vertices, each pair joined with probability 0.08), `dense` (random, 70 vertices, probability 0.5), `geometric` (120 random points in the unit square, joined when closer than 0.25) and `planted` (100 vertices secretly split into 6 groups; pairs in different groups are joined with probability 0.35, pairs in the same group never, so 6 colours suffice). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is colours used / the fewest colours known for that graph - 1, in % (for `planted`, the known 6 or fewer). Colour counts are small integers, so one colour more or less moves an instance's gap by roughly 10-25%.

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

import numpy as np
import math

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Saturation scaled by the fraction of uncoloured neighbours already coloured, reward for candidates that sit in a small closed neighbourhood."""
    k = neighbor_colors.shape[0]
    if neighbor_colors.shape[1] == 0:
        # no colours yet: use degree-based signal
        d = degree.astype(float)
        return (d - d.mean()) / (d.std() + 1e-9)
    sat = (neighbor_colors > 0).sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    colored_neigh = neighbor_colors.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    uncolored_neigh = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    total_neigh = colored_neigh + uncolored_neigh
    frac_colored = colored_neigh / (total_neigh + 1e-9)
    # reward high saturation concentrated in a small neighbourhood
    closed = total_neigh + 1.0
    val = sat * frac_colored / np.sqrt(closed)
    m = val.mean()
    s = val.std()
    return (val - m) / (s + 1e-9)
feature.measures: Saturation scaled by the fraction of uncoloured neighbours already coloured, reward for candidates that sit in a small closed neighbourhood.

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Fraction of a candidate's colour-closed neighbourhood already saturated by each forbidden colour, weighted by how tight the fit is (DSATUR-like pressure blended with saturation density)."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    # saturation: number of distinct colours among neighbours
    sat = (neighbor_colors > 0).sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    # uncoloured degree (potential future conflicts)
    uncol_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    # total neighbours = coloured (sum of row) + uncoloured
    coloured_deg = neighbor_colors.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    total_deg = coloured_deg + uncol_deg
    # saturation ratio: how close to being fully blocked across used colours
    sat_ratio = sat / np.maximum(c, 1.0)
    # tightness: fraction of neighbour mass concentrated on already-used colours
    used_mass = np.where(neighbor_colors > 0, neighbor_colors, 0).sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    tight = used_mass / np.maximum(coloured_deg, 1.0)
    # conflict density: coloured neighbours per total neighbour
    density = coloured_deg / np.maximum(total_deg, 1.0)
    # combine: high saturation, high tightness, low remaining uncoloured degree pressure
    val = sat_ratio * tight + 0.5 * density
    return np.clip(val, 0.0, 1.0)
feature.measures: Fraction of a candidate's colour-closed neighbourhood already saturated by each forbidden colour, weighted by how tight the fit is (DSATUR-like pressure blended with saturation density).

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Fraction of each candidate's uncoloured neighbours that are adjacent to each other (local density among the still-uncoloured)."""
    k = adjacency.shape[0]
    if k == 0:
        return np.zeros(0)
    uncolored_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    # number of edges among neighbours of v, via adjacency^2 restricted appropriately
    a = adjacency.astype(float)
    tri = np.einsum('ij,ij->i', a @ a, a)  # twice the number of triangles through v
    triangles = 0.5 * tri
    denom = uncolored_deg * (uncolored_deg - 1.0)
    density = np.where(denom > 0, 2.0 * triangles / np.maximum(denom, 1.0), 0.0)
    return np.nan_to_num(density, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0)

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

# The problem: Graph colouring: choose the order to colour vertices

Colour every vertex of a graph so that no two adjacent vertices share a colour, using as few colours as possible.

The colouring is built one vertex at a time. At each step the policy picks which uncoloured vertex to colour next; that vertex then automatically gets the smallest colour (colours are numbered 0, 1, 2, ...) not already used by one of its coloured neighbours. A new colour is opened only when every existing colour is taken by some neighbour. So the policy decides only the **order**, and the order decides how many colours are needed.

One **decision** = choosing the next vertex. The **candidates** are all uncoloured vertices, in index order. Vertices are numbered at random, so the index carries no information. When one vertex is left it is taken automatically.

Four training families: `sparse` (random graphs, 120 vertices, each pair joined with probability 0.08), `dense` (random, 70 vertices, probability 0.5), `geometric` (120 random points in the unit square, joined when closer than 0.25) and `planted` (100 vertices secretly split into 6 groups; pairs in different groups are joined with probability 0.35, pairs in the same group never, so 6 colours suffice). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is colours used / the fewest colours known for that graph - 1, in % (for `planted`, the known 6 or fewer). Colour counts are small integers, so one colour more or less moves an instance's gap by roughly 10-25%.

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Size of the class a candidate would actually join (first free colour), normalised by the largest class; -1 if it would open a new colour."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    free = (neighbor_colors == 0)
    has_free = free.any(axis=1)
    j = np.where(has_free, free.argmax(axis=1), c)
    join = np.where(j < c, color_sizes[np.minimum(j, c - 1)], 0.0)
    gain = join / np.maximum(color_sizes.max(), 1)
    return np.where(j < c, gain, -1.0)
```

It computes, per candidate, the size of the existing colour class it would actually join (the first free colour, i.e. the colour it would receive), divided by the largest current class size, with a hard floor of -1 for candidates that would be forced to open a new colour; when no colours exist yet it returns zeros.

# The problem: Graph colouring: choose the order to colour vertices

Colour every vertex of a graph so that no two adjacent vertices share a colour, using as few colours as possible.

The colouring is built one vertex at a time. At each step the policy picks which uncoloured vertex to colour next; that vertex then automatically gets the smallest colour (colours are numbered 0, 1, 2, ...) not already used by one of its coloured neighbours. A new colour is opened only when every existing colour is taken by some neighbour. So the policy decides only the **order**, and the order decides how many colours are needed.

One **decision** = choosing the next vertex. The **candidates** are all uncoloured vertices, in index order. Vertices are numbered at random, so the index carries no information. When one vertex is left it is taken automatically.

Four training families: `sparse` (random graphs, 120 vertices, each pair joined with probability 0.08), `dense` (random, 70 vertices, probability 0.5), `geometric` (120 random points in the unit square, joined when closer than 0.25) and `planted` (100 vertices secretly split into 6 groups; pairs in different groups are joined with probability 0.35, pairs in the same group never, so 6 colours suffice). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is colours used / the fewest colours known for that graph - 1, in % (for `planted`, the known 6 or fewer). Colour counts are small integers, so one colour more or less moves an instance's gap by roughly 10-25%.

```

The colour a candidate would get is the first column that is 0 in its row, or c (a new colour) if none is.
- `adjacency`: shape (k, k), bool: which candidates are adjacent to each other (the graph restricted to the uncoloured vertices; symmetric, False on the diagonal).
- `degree`: shape (k,), int: each candidate's degree in the whole graph (coloured + uncoloured neighbours).
- `color_sizes`: shape (c,), int: how many vertices have each colour so far.
- The whole graph has n = k + color_sizes.sum() vertices.
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c')). The highest-scoring candidate is coloured next.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Negative (normalised) count of uncoloured neighbours that lose the colour a candidate would take."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    Af = adjacency.astype(float)
    E = (neighbor_colors == 0).astype(float)          # (k, c): colours still available per candidate
    S = Af @ E                                        # (k, c): uncoloured neighbours that could take each colour
    free = (neighbor_colors == 0).any(axis=1)         # candidate can take an existing colour
    j = np.where(free, (neighbor_colors == 0).argmax(axis=1), c)  # colour it would get
    d_un = Af.sum(axis=1)                             # uncoloured neighbours
    damage = np.where(free, S[np.arange(k), np.minimum(j, c - 1)], d_un)
    return -damage / (damage.max() + 1e-9)
```

It computes, per candidate, the negated normalised number of uncoloured neighbours that would lose the colour the candidate is about to take (all uncoloured neighbours when a new colour is opened), returning zeros when no colour exists yet; I read "could still take j but for this candidate" as the count of uncoloured neighbours with column j zero, exactly as the experiment's formula specifies.

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Concentration of colour pressure: how much of a candidate's coloured-neighbour mass sits in its single most-used colour, scaled by the size of the colour class that colour belongs to and by how many distinct colours it touches."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    nbr = neighbor_colors.astype(float)
    row_sum = nbr.sum(axis=1)
    row_max = nbr.max(axis=1)
    touched = (nbr > 0).sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    # which colour dominates each row
    dom = nbr.argmax(axis=1)
    # size of that dominant colour class, normalised by total coloured vertices so far
    total_colored = np.maximum(color_sizes.sum(), 1.0)
    dom_size = color_sizes[dom].astype(float) / total_colored
    concentration = row_max / np.maximum(row_sum, 1.0)
    # spread factor: many distinct colours touched means the candidate is boxed in
    spread = touched / np.maximum(c, 1.0)
    raw = concentration * (0.5 + dom_size) * (1.0 + spread)
    return np.where(row_sum > 0, raw / 2.0, 0.0)
feature.measures: Concentration of colour pressure: how much of a candidate's coloured-neighbour mass sits in its single most-used colour, scaled by the size of the colour class that colour belongs to and by how many distinct colours it touches.

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Saturation count mixed with a bonus for candidates that can still join an existing colour (no new colour forced)."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    touched = (neighbor_colors > 0).sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    # a candidate is "free" if at least one existing colour is not taken by any neighbour
    has_free = (neighbor_colors == 0).any(axis=1).astype(float)
    uncolored_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    total_deg = np.maximum(degree.astype(float), 1.0)
    frac_uncol = uncolored_deg / total_deg
    # weight saturation by how open the candidate still is, and reward free-existing-colour candidates
    reward = has_free * (1.0 + frac_uncol)
    raw = touched * (1.0 + frac_uncol) - 0.5 * (1.0 - has_free) * frac_uncol
    norm = np.maximum(c, 1.0)
    return (raw + reward) / (norm + 1.0)
feature.measures: Saturation count mixed with a bonus for candidates that can still join an existing colour (no new colour forced).

        return np.zeros(k)
    touched = (neighbor_colors > 0).sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    # a candidate is "free" if at least one existing colour is not taken by any neighbour
    has_free = (neighbor_colors == 0).any(axis=1).astype(float)
    uncolored_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    total_deg = np.maximum(degree.astype(float), 1.0)
    frac_uncol = uncolored_deg / total_deg
    # weight saturation by how open the candidate still is, and reward free-existing-colour candidates
    reward = has_free * (1.0 + frac_uncol)
    raw = touched * (1.0 + frac_uncol) - 0.5 * (1.0 - has_free) * frac_uncol
    norm = np.maximum(c, 1.0)
    return (raw + reward) / (norm + 1.0)

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Graph colouring: choose the order to colour vertices

Colour every vertex of a graph so that no two adjacent vertices share a colour, using as few colours as possible.

The colouring is built one vertex at a time. At each step the policy picks which uncoloured vertex to colour next; that vertex then automatically gets the smallest colour (colours are numbered 0, 1, 2, ...) not already used by one of its coloured neighbours. A new colour is opened only when every existing colour is taken by some neighbour. So the policy decides only the **order**, and the order decides how many colours are needed.

One **decision** = choosing the next vertex. The **candidates** are all uncoloured vertices, in index order. Vertices are numbered at random, so the index carries no information. When one vertex is left it is taken automatically.

Four training families: `sparse` (random graphs, 120 vertices, each pair joined with probability 0.08), `dense` (random, 70 vertices, probability 0.5), `geometric` (120 random points in the unit square, joined when closer than 0.25) and `planted` (100 vertices secretly split into 6 groups; pairs in different groups are joined with probability 0.35, pairs in the same group never, so 6 colours suffice). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is colours used / the fewest colours known for that graph - 1, in % (for `planted`, the known 6 or fewer). Colour counts are small integers, so one colour more or less moves an instance's gap by roughly 10-25%.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `neighbor_colors`: shape (k, c), int: for each candidate (uncoloured vertex, index order) and each colour used so far, how many of its neighbours already have that colour. c = number of colours used so far (c = 0 at the first decision: the array has shape (k, 0)). The colour a candidate would get is the first column that is 0 in its row, or c (a new colour) if none is.
- `adjacency`: shape (k, k), bool: which candidates are adjacent to each other (the graph restricted to the uncoloured vertices; symmetric, False on the diagonal).
- `degree`: shape (k,), int: each candidate's degree in the whole graph (coloured + uncoloured neighbours).
- `color_sizes`: shape (c,), int: how many vertices have each colour so far.
- The whole graph has n = k + color_sizes.sum() vertices.
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c')). The highest-scoring candidate is coloured next.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Saturation weighted by the fraction of colour choices still open to a candidate (saturation times remaining freedom)."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        # no colours yet: prefer high-degree hubs, normalised
        uncolored_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
        return uncolored_deg / (uncolored_deg.max() + 1.0)
    touched = (neighbor_colors > 0).sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    # how many of the c colours are still usable for this candidate
    free = np.maximum(c - touched, 0.0)
    # saturating candidates with few free colours are urgent
    urgency = touched / (np.maximum(c, 1.0) + 1.0)
    # but also reward candidates that constrain many uncoloured neighbours
    uncolored_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    reach = uncolored_deg / (uncolored_deg.max() + 1.0)
    # geometric blend: urgency dominant, reach as tie-breaker, freedom dampens
    raw = urgency * (1.0 + reach) 
    damp = 1.0 / (1.0 + free)
    return raw * damp

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """For candidates that must take an existing colour: prefer the colour class whose members are fewest among its neighbours, scaled by class sparsity; 0 if it opens a new colour."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    nc = neighbor_colors.astype(float)
    blocked = (nc > 0).any(axis=1)
    # For each candidate take the least-contested forbidden colour (min positive count)
    big = np.where(nc > 0, nc, np.inf)
    min_conflict = big.min(axis=1)
    min_conflict = np.where(np.isfinite(min_conflict), min_conflict, 0.0)
    # sparsity of the chosen class: how few vertices already hold that colour
    sizes = color_sizes.astype(float)
    # weight each colour by inverse size; pick the colour that is both least-contested and sparse
    inv_size = 1.0 / np.maximum(sizes, 1.0)
    score = np.where(nc > 0, nc * inv_size[None, :], np.inf)
    best = score.min(axis=1)
    best = np.where(np.isfinite(best), best, 0.0)
    total_deg = np.maximum(degree.astype(float), 1.0)
    raw = min_conflict * best
    return np.where(blocked, -raw / total_deg, 0.0)

    free = np.maximum(c - touched, 0.0)
    # saturating candidates with few free colours are urgent
    urgency = touched / (np.maximum(c, 1.0) + 1.0)
    # but also reward candidates that constrain many uncoloured neighbours
    uncolored_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    reach = uncolored_deg / (uncolored_deg.max() + 1.0)
    # geometric blend: urgency dominant, reach as tie-breaker, freedom dampens
    raw = urgency * (1.0 + reach) 
    damp = 1.0 / (1.0 + free)
    return raw * damp

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """For candidates forced to open a new colour, how many uncoloured neighbours are themselves NOT yet saturated (still have a free existing colour), scaled by neighbourhood size."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    uncolored_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    n = k + color_sizes.sum()
    if c == 0:
        return uncolored_deg / (n + 1.0)
    # a candidate is "forced" if every existing colour is already taken by a neighbour
    forced = (neighbor_colors > 0).all(axis=1)
    # how many of the candidate's uncoloured neighbours are themselves unsaturated
    # (i.e. still have at least one colour free). Saturated neighbours gain nothing more from waiting.
    neigh_saturated = (neighbor_colors > 0).sum(axis=1)  # distinct colours touching each candidate
    # Build per-candidate count of unsaturated uncoloured neighbours via adjacency.
    # ranks of candidates; use matrix product with indicator of "candidate is unsaturated"
    neighbor_has_free = (neighbor_colors > 0).sum(axis=1) < c
    unsat_uncolored = adjacency.astype(float) @ neighbor_has_free.astype(float)
    # only count the forced ones; normalise by total neighbourhood to keep bounded
    raw = np.where(forced, unsat_uncolored, 0.0)
    return raw / (uncolored_deg + 1.0)

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """For candidates that must take an existing colour: prefer the colour class whose members are fewest among its neighbours, scaled by class sparsity; 0 if it opens a new colour."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    nc = neighbor_colors.astype(float)
    blocked = (nc > 0).any(axis=1)
    # For each candidate take the least-contested forbidden colour (min positive count)
    big = np.where(nc > 0, nc, np.inf)
    min_conflict = big.min(axis=1)
    min_conflict = np.where(np.isfinite(min_conflict), min_conflict, 0.0)
    # sparsity of the chosen class: how few vertices already hold that colour
    sizes = color_sizes.astype(float)
    # weight each colour by inverse size; pick the colour that is both least-contested and sparse
    inv_size = 1.0 / np.maximum(sizes, 1.0)
    score = np.where(nc > 0, nc * inv_size[None, :], np.inf)
    best = score.min(axis=1)
    best = np.where(np.isfinite(best), best, 0.0)
    total_deg = np.maximum(degree.astype(float), 1.0)
    raw = min_conflict * best
    return np.where(blocked, -raw / total_deg, 0.0)
feature.measures: For candidates that must take an existing colour: prefer the colour class whose members are fewest among its neighbours, scaled by class sparsity; 0 if it opens a new colour.

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Saturation weighted by the inverse size of the smallest available colour class a candidate could join, else max pressure for new-colour candidates."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        # No colours yet: prefer vertices whose uncoloured neighbourhood is large (constrain early)
        return adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float) / (k + 1.0)
    blocked = neighbor_colors > 0
    # available colour classes: those not blocked by any neighbour
    avail = ~blocked  # (k, c)
    sizes = color_sizes.astype(float)  # (c,)
    # inverse-size preference: small existing classes are cheaper to extend
    inv_size = 1.0 / (sizes + 1.0)
    # masked weight per (candidate, colour): only available colours contribute
    masked = np.where(avail, inv_size[None, :], 0.0)
    best_fit = masked.max(axis=1)  # best (smallest class) available colour
    any_avail = avail.any(axis=1)
    # saturation: distinct colours touched
    sat = blocked.sum(axis=1).astype(float) / (c + 1.0)
    # new-colour candidates: pressure from uncoloured neighbourhood
    uncolored_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    n = k + color_sizes.sum()
    new_press = uncolored_deg / (n + 1.0)
    out = np.where(any_avail, sat * best_fit, new_press * (1.0 + sat))
    return out

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Negative mean, over a candidate's uncoloured neighbours, of the number of colours still legal for them after the candidate is coloured (normalised)."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    touched = (neighbor_colors > 0).sum(1)
    legal = (c + 1.0) - touched
    free_mat = (neighbor_colors == 0)
    taken = np.where(free_mat.any(1), free_mat.argmax(1), c)
    onehot = np.zeros((k, c + 1))
    onehot[np.arange(k), taken] = 1.0
    loss = onehot[:, :c] @ free_mat.T.astype(float)
    A = adjacency.astype(float)
    nb = A.sum(1)
    after = A @ legal - (A * loss).sum(1)
    return -(after / (nb + 1.0)) / (c + 2.0)

The full one-step lookahead is: after candidate i takes its colour, how many colours in total remain legal for its uncoloured neighbours (colours 0..c minus those a neighbour already uses, minus the one i just took if it was free for that neighbour). Minimising that mean budget picks vertices that saturate their neighbourhood without wasting a colour, and if the ordering of candidates by budget differs from saturation the optimiser can combine them.

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Graph colouring: choose the order to colour vertices

Colour every vertex of a graph so that no two adjacent vertices share a colour, using as few colours as possible.

The colouring is built one vertex at a time. At each step the policy picks which uncoloured vertex to colour next; that vertex then automatically gets the smallest colour (colours are numbered 0, 1, 2, ...) not already used by one of its coloured neighbours. A new colour is opened only when every existing colour is taken by some neighbour. So the policy decides only the **order**, and the order decides how many colours are needed.

One **decision** = choosing the next vertex. The **candidates** are all uncoloured vertices, in index order. Vertices are numbered at random, so the index carries no information. When one vertex is left it is taken automatically.

Four training families: `sparse` (random graphs, 120 vertices, each pair joined with probability 0.08), `dense` (random, 70 vertices, probability 0.5), `geometric` (120 random points in the unit square, joined when closer than 0.25) and `planted` (100 vertices secretly split into 6 groups; pairs in different groups are joined with probability 0.35, pairs in the same group never, so 6 colours suffice). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is colours used / the fewest colours known for that graph - 1, in % (for `planted`, the known 6 or fewer). Colour counts are small integers, so one colour more or less moves an instance's gap by roughly 10-25%.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `neighbor_colors`: shape (k, c), int: for each candidate (uncoloured vertex, index order) and each colour used so far, how many of its neighbours already have that colour. c = number of colours used so far (c = 0 at the first decision: the array has shape (k, 0)). The colour a candidate would get is the first column that is 0 in its row, or c (a new colour) if none is.
- `adjacency`: shape (k, k), bool: which candidates are adjacent to each other (the graph restricted to the uncoloured vertices; symmetric, False on the diagonal).
- `degree`: shape (k,), int: each candidate's degree in the whole graph (coloured + uncoloured neighbours).
- `color_sizes`: shape (c,), int: how many vertices have each colour so far.
- The whole graph has n = k + color_sizes.sum() vertices.
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c')). The highest-scoring candidate is coloured next.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):

    nbr_blocked = (neighbor_colors > 0).sum(axis=1).astype(float)  # (k,)

    adj = adjacency.astype(float)

    # weight by how many uncoloured neighbours would be affected
    frac = uncolored_deg / (k + 1.0)
    return tightness * frac

# The problem: Graph colouring: choose the order to colour vertices

Colour every vertex of a graph so that no two adjacent vertices share a colour, using as few colours as possible.

The colouring is built one vertex at a time. At each step the policy picks which uncoloured vertex to colour next; that vertex then automatically gets the smallest colour (colours are numbered 0, 1, 2, ...) not already used by one of its coloured neighbours. A new colour is opened only when every existing colour is taken by some neighbour. So the policy decides only the **order**, and the order decides how many colours are needed.

One **decision** = choosing the next vertex. The **candidates** are all uncoloured vertices, in index order. Vertices are numbered at random, so the index carries no information. When one vertex is left it is taken automatically.

Four training families: `sparse` (random graphs, 120 vertices, each pair joined with probability 0.08), `dense` (random, 70 vertices, probability 0.5), `geometric` (120 random points in the unit square, joined when closer than 0.25) and `planted` (100 vertices secretly split into 6 groups; pairs in different groups are joined with probability 0.35, pairs in the same group never, so 6 colours suffice). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is colours used / the fewest colours known for that graph - 1, in % (for `planted`, the known 6 or fewer). Colour counts are small integers, so one colour more or less moves an instance's gap by roughly 10-25%.

Colour every vertex of a graph so that no two adjacent vertices share a colour, using as few colours as possible.

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Sparsity of the candidate's uncoloured neighbourhood: 1 - (edges among uncoloured neighbours / possible pairs), scaled by neighbourhood size."""
    A = adjacency.astype(float)

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Saturation of a candidate measured against the colours it still allows its uncoloured neighbours: mean over uncoloured neighbours of (colours legal for the neighbour after this candidate is coloured), normalised."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    touched = (neighbor_colors > 0).astype(float)          # (k, c) colours touching candidate
    # colours touching each candidate, expanded along neighbour axis via adjacency
    # for each candidate i, for each uncoloured neighbour j: colours blocked for j if i took colour t
    # approximate: a neighbour j loses a colour when j has no other vertex of that colour adjacent besides i
    # We use the candidate's touched colours as the colours it could take (first free), and the
    # neighbour's legal count after i is coloured with its first-free colour.
    # first free colour index per candidate
    free = (neighbor_colors == 0)
    has_free = free.any(axis=1)
    first_free = np.where(has_free, free.argmax(axis=1), c)  # (k,)
    # colour candidate i would take = first_free[i]; if == c, opens new colour, blocks nothing extra
    # for neighbour j, the colour i takes becomes illegal for j if j is adjacent to i and j doesn't
    # already have that colour forbidden... it does become forbidden unless j already has a neighbour of that colour.
    # Build (k,k) mask: neighbour j would lose colour first_free[i] iff adjacency[i,j] and that colour
    # is not already among j's touched colours (i.e. j doesn't already forbid it).
    new_blocks = np.zeros((k, k))
    for t in range(c + 1):
        cand = first_free == t
        if not cand.any():
            continue
        # candidate i with colour t blocks colour t for neighbour j if j is adjacent and j doesn't already forbid t
        forbids_t = touched[:, t] if t < c else np.zeros(k)
        block_row = adjacency[cand] & (forbids_t[None, :] < 0.5)
        if t == c:
            # opening a new colour: nothing new forbidden for neighbours beyond the new colour itself
            pass
        new_blocks[cand] = block_row.astype(float)
    # colours currently legal for each candidate (uncoloured neighbours perspective)
    legal_now = (c - touched.sum(axis=1)).astype(float)  # (k,)
    nb_count = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    # mean legal-after over uncoloured neighbours
    lost = new_blocks @ np.ones(k)  # not used; compute directly:
    # sum over neighbours of legal_now[j] - new_blocks[i,j]
    sum_legal = adjacency @ legal_now
    sum_block = new_blocks.sum(axis=1)
    mean_after = np.where(nb_count > 0, (sum_legal - sum_block) / np.maximum(nb_count, 1.0), 0.0)
    # scale by saturation pressure: candidates touching more colours (more urgent) get amplified
    sat_frac = touched.sum(axis=1) / np.maximum(c, 1.0)
    return (mean_after / (c + 1.0)) * (1.0 + sat_frac)

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """For candidates that must open a new colour, the count of their uncoloured neighbours that are themselves already saturated (all used colours forbidden), normalised; else a small negative for how compressible a candidate's options are."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        uncolored_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
        return uncolored_deg / (k + 1.0)
    # a candidate must open a new colour if every used colour is taken by some neighbour
    blocked = (neighbor_colors > 0).all(axis=1)
    opens_new = blocked
    # saturation of each candidate's uncoloured neighbours: does each neighbour have all colours forbidden?
    # a neighbour j of candidate i is "saturated" if every colour used so far touches j via some neighbour.
    # neighbor_colors rows are per-candidate; adjacency links candidates. Approximate neighbour saturation
    # via the candidate's own colour-forbidden profile being fully dense on its neighbours' perspective.
    # Count how many distinct colours a candidate still has available (0 => it opens new).
    avail = (neighbor_colors == 0).sum(axis=1).astype(float)  # legal existing colours
    uncolored_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    # neighbours that are one step from saturation: those sharing the same tightest forbidden set.
    # proxy: number of a candidate's uncoloured neighbours times how few options that neighbour has left.
    # estimate neighbour options by column of forbidden colour sets among candidates.
    # vectorised: for each candidate, sum over its neighbours of (1 / (1 + their available colours)).
    inv_avail = 1.0 / (1.0 + avail)  # higher when neighbour is close to forced
    neigh_pressure = adjacency.astype(float) @ inv_avail  # sum over uncoloured neighbours
    n = k + color_sizes.sum()
    pressure_norm = neigh_pressure / (n + 1.0)
    # for candidates that open a new colour, reward pressure they impose on constrained neighbours
    return np.where(opens_new, pressure_norm, -inv_avail * (uncolored_deg / (n + 1.0)))

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """For the colour a candidate would take, the fraction of its uncoloured neighbours that are the last remaining user of that colour, i.e. would be forced to open a new colour."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    Af = adjacency.astype(float)
    E = (neighbor_colors == 0)                        # (k, c) bool: colour still legal per candidate
    avail = E.sum(axis=1)                             # colours still legal per candidate
    free = avail > 0
    j = np.where(free, E.argmax(axis=1), c)           # the colour it would take
    d_un = Af.sum(axis=1)
    # For each candidate u, look at its uncoloured neighbours v and whether v would lose colour j_u.
    # v loses it if adjacency[u,v] and the only zero in row v is column j_u -> count via matrix.
    # S[v, col] = number of v's uncoloured neighbours that could take col
    S = Af @ E.astype(float)                          # (k, c)
    # v is "last user" of colour col if S[v, col] == 1 (only u could take it) and E[v, col] is True
    lastuser = (S <= 1.0) & E                         # (k, c) bool
    # For u with chosen colour j_u, count neighbours v that are last users of j_u
    # Gather column j_u of lastuser, then count adjacencies to those v
    jj = np.minimum(j, c - 1)
    col_last = lastuser[np.arange(k), jj].astype(float)  # (k,): is v a last user of j_u
    # u's neighbours that are last users of j_u
    forced = Af @ col_last
    denom = np.maximum(d_un, 1.0)
    val = np.where(free, forced / denom, np.ones(k))
    return -val
feature.measures: For the colour a candidate would take, the fraction of its uncoloured neighbours that are the last remaining user of that colour, i.e. would be forced to open a new colour.

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Saturation of a candidate measured against the colours it still allows its uncoloured neighbours: mean over uncoloured neighbours of (colours legal for the neighbour after this candidate is coloured), normalised."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    touched = (neighbor_colors > 0).astype(float)          # (k, c) colours touching candidate
    # colours touching each candidate, expanded along neighbour axis via adjacency
    # for each candidate i, for each uncoloured neighbour j: colours blocked for j if i took colour t
    # approximate: a neighbour j loses a colour when j has no other vertex of that colour adjacent besides i
    # We use the candidate's touched colours as the colours it could take (first free), and the
    # neighbour's legal count after i is coloured with its first-free colour.
    # first free colour index per candidate
    free = (neighbor_colors == 0)
    has_free = free.any(axis=1)
    first_free = np.where(has_free, free.argmax(axis=1), c)  # (k,)
    # colour candidate i would take = first_free[i]; if == c, opens new colour, blocks nothing extra
    # for neighbour j, the colour i takes becomes illegal for j if j is adjacent to i and j doesn't
    # already have that colour forbidden... it does become forbidden unless j already has a neighbour of that colour.
    # Build (k,k) mask: neighbour j would lose colour first_free[i] iff adjacency[i,j] and that colour
    # is not already among j's touched colours (i.e. j doesn't already forbid it).
    new_blocks = np.zeros((k, k))
    for t in range(c + 1):
        cand = first_free == t
        if not cand.any():
            continue
        # candidate i with colour t blocks colour t for neighbour j if j is adjacent and j doesn't already forbid t
        forbids_t = touched[:, t] if t < c else np.zeros(k)
        block_row = adjacency[cand] & (forbids_t[None, :] < 0.5)
        if t == c:
            # opening a new colour: nothing new forbidden for neighbours beyond the new colour itself
            pass
        new_blocks[cand] = block_row.astype(float)
    # colours currently legal for each candidate (uncoloured neighbours perspective)
    legal_now = (c - touched.sum(axis=1)).astype(float)  # (k,)
    nb_count = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    # mean legal-after over uncoloured neighbours
    lost = new_blocks @ np.ones(k)  # not used; compute directly:
    # sum over neighbours of legal_now[j] - new_blocks[i,j]
    sum_legal = adjacency @ legal_now
    sum_block = new_blocks.sum(axis=1)
    mean_after = np.where(nb_count > 0, (sum_legal - sum_block) / np.maximum(nb_count, 1.0), 0.0)
    # scale by saturation pressure: candidates touching more colours (more urgent) get amplified
    sat_frac = touched.sum(axis=1) / np.maximum(c, 1.0)
    return (mean_after / (c + 1.0)) * (1.0 + sat_frac)
feature.measures: Saturation of a candidate measured against the colours it still allows its uncoloured neighbours: mean over uncoloured neighbours of (colours legal for the neighbour after this candidate is coloured), normalised.

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """For candidates that must open a new colour, the count of their uncoloured neighbours that are themselves already saturated (all used colours forbidden), normalised; else a small negative for how compressible a candidate's options are."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        uncolored_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
        return uncolored_deg / (k + 1.0)
    # a candidate must open a new colour if every used colour is taken by some neighbour
    blocked = (neighbor_colors > 0).all(axis=1)
    opens_new = blocked
    # saturation of each candidate's uncoloured neighbours: does each neighbour have all colours forbidden?
    # a neighbour j of candidate i is "saturated" if every colour used so far touches j via some neighbour.
    # neighbor_colors rows are per-candidate; adjacency links candidates. Approximate neighbour saturation
    # via the candidate's own colour-forbidden profile being fully dense on its neighbours' perspective.
    # Count how many distinct colours a candidate still has available (0 => it opens new).
    avail = (neighbor_colors == 0).sum(axis=1).astype(float)  # legal existing colours
    uncolored_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    # neighbours that are one step from saturation: those sharing the same tightest forbidden set.
    # proxy: number of a candidate's uncoloured neighbours times how few options that neighbour has left.
    # estimate neighbour options by column of forbidden colour sets among candidates.
    # vectorised: for each candidate, sum over its neighbours of (1 / (1 + their available colours)).
    inv_avail = 1.0 / (1.0 + avail)  # higher when neighbour is close to forced
    neigh_pressure = adjacency.astype(float) @ inv_avail  # sum over uncoloured neighbours
    n = k + color_sizes.sum()
    pressure_norm = neigh_pressure / (n + 1.0)
    # for candidates that open a new colour, reward pressure they impose on constrained neighbours
    return np.where(opens_new, pressure_norm, -inv_avail * (uncolored_deg / (n + 1.0)))
feature.measures: For candidates that must open a new colour, the count of their uncoloured neighbours that are themselves already saturated (all used colours forbidden), normalised; else a small negative for how compressible a candidate's options are.

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """For the colour a candidate would take, the fraction of its uncoloured neighbours that are the last remaining user of that colour, i.e. would be forced to open a new colour."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    Af = adjacency.astype(float)
    E = (neighbor_colors == 0)                        # (k, c) bool: colour still legal per candidate
    avail = E.sum(axis=1)                             # colours still legal per candidate
    free = avail > 0
    j = np.where(free, E.argmax(axis=1), c)           # the colour it would take
    d_un = Af.sum(axis=1)
    # For each candidate u, look at its uncoloured neighbours v and whether v would lose colour j_u.
    # v loses it if adjacency[u,v] and the only zero in row v is column j_u -> count via matrix.
    # S[v, col] = number of v's uncoloured neighbours that could take col
    S = Af @ E.astype(float)                          # (k, c)
    # v is "last user" of colour col if S[v, col] == 1 (only u could take it) and E[v, col] is True
    lastuser = (S <= 1.0) & E                         # (k, c) bool
    # For u with chosen colour j_u, count neighbours v that are last users of j_u
    # Gather column j_u of lastuser, then count adjacencies to those v
    jj = np.minimum(j, c - 1)
    col_last = lastuser[np.arange(k), jj].astype(float)  # (k,): is v a last user of j_u
    # u's neighbours that are last users of j_u
    forced = Af @ col_last
    denom = np.maximum(d_un, 1.0)
    val = np.where(free, forced / denom, np.ones(k))
    return -val
feature.measures: For the colour a candidate would take, the fraction of its uncoloured neighbours that are the last remaining user of that colour, i.e. would be forced to open a new colour.

import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Sparsity of the candidate's uncoloured neighbourhood: 1 - (edges among uncoloured neighbours / possible pairs), scaled by neighbourhood size."""
    A = adjacency.astype(float)
    d = A.sum(axis=1)
    C = A @ A
    tri = 0.5 * (A * C).sum(axis=1)  # edges among the candidate's uncoloured neighbours
    pairs = d * (d - 1.0) / 2.0
    density = tri / np.maximum(pairs, 1.0)  # in [0,1]
    sparsity = 1.0 - density
    # weight by how much neighbourhood there is to be sparse: a lone vertex has no pairs,
    # so its sparsity is meaningless; scale by pairs/(pairs+1) in [0,1)
    confidence = pairs / (pairs + 1.0)
    return sparsity * confidence

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Graph colouring: choose the order to colour vertices

Colour every vertex of a graph so that no two adjacent vertices share a colour, using as few colours as possible.

The colouring is built one vertex at a time. At each step the policy picks which uncoloured vertex to colour next; that vertex then automatically gets the smallest colour (colours are numbered 0, 1, 2, ...) not already used by one of its coloured neighbours. A new colour is opened only when every existing colour is taken by some neighbour. So the policy decides only the **order**, and the order decides how many colours are needed.

One **decision** = choosing the next vertex. The **candidates** are all uncoloured vertices, in index order. Vertices are numbered at random, so the index carries no information. When one vertex is left it is taken automatically.

Four training families: `sparse` (random graphs, 120 vertices, each pair joined with probability 0.08), `dense` (random, 70 vertices, probability 0.5), `geometric` (120 random points in the unit square, joined when closer than 0.25) and `planted` (100 vertices secretly split into 6 groups; pairs in different groups are joined with probability 0.35, pairs in the same group never, so 6 colours suffice). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is colours used / the fewest colours known for that graph - 1, in % (for `planted`, the known 6 or fewer). Colour counts are small integers, so one colour more or less moves an instance's gap by roughly 10-25%.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `neighbor_colors`: shape (k, c), int: for each candidate (uncoloured vertex, index order) and each colour used so far, how many of its neighbours already have that colour. c = number of colours used so far (c = 0 at the first decision: the array has shape (k, 0)). The colour a candidate would get is the first column that is 0 in its row, or c (a new colour) if none is.
- `adjacency`: shape (k, k), bool: which candidates are adjacent to each other (the graph restricted to the uncoloured vertices; symmetric, False on the diagonal).
- `degree`: shape (k,), int: each candidate's degree in the whole graph (coloured + uncoloured neighbours).
- `color_sizes`: shape (c,), int: how many vertices have each colour so far.
- The whole graph has n = k + color_sizes.sum() vertices.
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c')). The highest-scoring candidate is coloured next.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    k = degree.shape[0]
    m = color_sizes.sum()  # coloured count
    if m == 0:

    n = k + m

    non_adj = m - col_nghb
    baseline = m * (1.0 - degree / max(n-1,1))  # expected non-adjacency

```

system:
You are the **Mutator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You are the wide loop: you make bold, undirected variations and let the evaluator decide. You see the artefacts and their scores only; nobody tells you why anything works, on purpose, so the search doesn't narrow around one idea too early.

Each request asks you for **one** new candidate:

- **Vary a parent:** keep a thread of it, but change it boldly: a different form, a condition, a combination with something else. A timid tweak is wasted.
- **Fresh:** something that nothing on the scoreboard already does.

The **scoreboard** shows what was already evaluated and what happened to it (gain = how much better the result got; negative = worse). Don't reproduce any of it: disguised copies are detected and discarded without being evaluated.

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The policy is a weighted sum of **features** (measurements of a candidate). An optimiser fits the weights and signs, so never choose numbers or signs.

- **Varying a parent feature:** a different functional form, a condition (only for some decisions or some candidates), a combination with another quantity, a different normalisation. Tweaking a constant is wasted: the optimiser already tunes the weight.
- A feature that ranks candidates the same way as one on the scoreboard (including a sign flip or a monotone transform) is a duplicate.

# The problem: Graph colouring: choose the order to colour vertices

Colour every vertex of a graph so that no two adjacent vertices share a colour, using as few colours as possible.

The colouring is built one vertex at a time. a07: "saturation times (coloured neighbours / degree), plus count of neighbours about to be forced."

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    deg = np.maximum(degree.astype(float), 1.0)
    uncol_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    cn = deg - uncol_deg                     # coloured neighbours
    if c == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    sat_count = (neighbor_colors > 0).sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    sat = sat_count / c
    completion = cn / deg                    # fraction of closed neighbourhood already coloured
    free_cnt = c - sat_count                 # existing colours still legal for the candidate
    # uncoloured neighbours that have at most one existing colour left ("about to be forced")
    nbr_about_forced = adjacency @ ((free_cnt <= 1) & (uncol_deg > 0)).astype(float)
    nbr_about_forced = nbr_about_forced / np.maximum(uncol_deg, 1.0)
    return np.clip(sat * completion - 0.5 * nbr_about_forced, -1.0, 1.0)
```

**Feature 1: excess non-adjacency (a21)**

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Coloured-neighbour deficit: how much rarer a candidate's coloured neighbours are
    than its degree predicts (positive = fewer coloured neighbours than expected)."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    n = float(k + color_sizes.sum())
    m = n - k                                  # coloured vertices
    if m <= 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    deg = degree.astype(float)
    uncol_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    cn = np.maximum(deg - uncol_deg, 0.0)      # coloured neighbours
    expected = deg / max(n - 1.0, 1.0)         # expected coloured share of a neighbourhood
    actual = cn / m
    return np.clip(expected - actual, -1.0, 1.0)
```
Using n-1 in the denominator (a vertex has at most n-1 neighbours). Fine.

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Negative normalised index of the colour the candidate would take
    (first colour with no neighbour already using it; c if it opens a new colour)."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    free = neighbor_colors == 0                    # (k, c) legal existing colours
    first = np.where(free.any(axis=1), free.argmax(axis=1), c).astype(float)
    return -first / float(c)
```

def feature(neighbor_colors, adjacency, degree, color_sizes):
    """Saturation times closed-neighbourhood completion, minus the share of uncoloured
    neighbours that have only one existing colour left (would be pushed into a new one)."""
    k, c = neighbor_colors.shape
    if c == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    deg = np.maximum(degree.astype(float), 1.0)
    uncol_deg = adjacency.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    cn = np.maximum(deg - uncol_deg, 0.0)
    sat_count = (neighbor_colors > 0).sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    sat = sat_count / float(c)
    completion = cn / deg
    free_cnt = float(c) - sat_count                      # existing colours still legal
    almost_forced = ((free_cnt == 1.0) & (uncol_deg > 0)).astype(float)
    nbr_pressure = adjacency.astype(float) @ almost_forced
    nbr_pressure = nbr_pressure / np.maximum(uncol_deg, 1.0)
    return np.clip(sat * completion - 0.5 * nbr_pressure, -1.0, 1.0)

# The problem: Graph colouring: choose the order to colour vertices

Colour every vertex of a graph so that no two adjacent vertices share a colour, using as few colours as possible.

The colouring is built one vertex at a time. At each step the policy picks which uncoloured vertex to colour next; that vertex then automatically gets the smallest colour (colours are numbered 0, 1, 2, ...) not already used by one of its coloured neighbours. A new colour is opened only when every existing colour is taken by some neighbour. So the policy decides only the **order**, and the order decides how many colours are needed.

One **decision** = choosing the next vertex. The **candidates** are all uncoloured vertices, in index order. Vertices are numbered at random, so the index carries no information. When one vertex is left it is taken automatically.

Four training families: `sparse` (random graphs, 120 vertices, each pair joined with probability 0.08), `dense` (random, 70 vertices, probability 0.5), `geometric` (120 random points in the unit square, joined when closer than 0.25) and `planted` (100 vertices secretly split into 6 groups; pairs in different groups are joined with probability 0.35, pairs in the same group never, so 6 colours suffice). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is colours used / the fewest colours known for that graph - 1, in % (for `planted`, the known 6 or fewer). Colour counts are small integers, so one colour more or less moves an instance's gap by roughly 10-25%.
